claim: C4 photosynthesis has independently evolved from the ancestral C3 pathway in at least 60 plant lineages.
source: C4 photosynthesis has independently evolved from the ancestral C3 pathway in at least 60 plant lineages
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2011a in the introduction section.

claim: The polyphyletic appearance of C4 photosynthesis is associated with diverse and flexible evolutionary paths that group into four major trajectories.
source: the polyphyletic appearance of C4 photosynthesis is associated with diverse and flexible evolutionary paths that group into four major trajectories
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis and modeling presented in the manuscript, supported by data from 18 lineages and Bayesian analysis.

claim: A meta-analysis was conducted of 18 lineages containing species that use C3, C4, or intermediate C3–C4 forms of photosynthesis to parameterise a 16-dimensional phenotypic landscape.
source: We conducted a meta-analysis of 18 lineages containing species that use C3, C4, or intermediate C3–C4 forms of photosynthesis to parameterise a 16-dimensional phenotypic landscape.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology and data collection from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species.

claim: A novel Bayesian approach based on a hidden Markov model was developed and experimentally verified to predict how the C4 phenotype evolved.
source: We then developed and experimentally verified a novel Bayesian approach based on a hidden Markov model that predicts how the C4 phenotype evolved.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of the HMM-based Bayesian approach and its experimental verification through qPCR experiments.

claim: The alternative evolutionary histories underlying the appearance of C4 photosynthesis were determined by ancestral lineage and initial phenotypic alterations unrelated to photosynthesis.
source: The alternative evolutionary histories underlying the appearance of C4 photosynthesis were determined by ancestral lineage and initial phenotypic alterations unrelated to photosynthesis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis showing different evolutionary trajectories for monocots vs. eudicots and NADP-ME vs. NAD-ME subtypes.

claim: The order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible and driven by non-photosynthetic drivers.
source: We conclude that the order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible and driven by non-photosynthetic drivers.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the contingency analysis showing no inflexible linkage between traits and the finding that anatomical changes precede biochemical changes.

claim: This flexibility in evolutionary pathways will have facilitated the convergent evolution of C4 photosynthesis.
source: This flexibility will have facilitated the convergent evolution of this complex trait.
evidence: This is a logical inference drawn from the finding of multiple flexible evolutionary pathways.

claim: The C4 pathway is estimated to have first evolved between 32 and 25 million years ago.
source: The C4 pathway is estimated to have first evolved between 32 and 25 million years ago (Christin et al., 2011b)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Christin et al., 2011b.

claim: C4 photosynthesis evolved in response to multiple ecological drivers, including decreasing atmospheric CO2 concentration.
source: The C4 pathway is estimated to have first evolved between 32 and 25 million years ago (Christin et al., 2011b) in response to multiple ecological drivers, including decreasing atmospheric CO2 concentration (Vicentini et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Vicentini et al., 2008.

claim: In C4 plants, photosynthetic efficiency is improved compared with C3 species because modifications to leaves lead to higher concentrations of CO2 around RuBisCO.
source: In C4 plants, photosynthetic efficiency is improved compared with C3 species because significant alterations to leaf anatomy, cell biology and biochemistry lead to higher concentrations of CO2 around the primary carboxylase RuBisCO Slack and Hatch, 1967; Langdale, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Slack and Hatch, 1967 and Langdale, 2011.

claim: The morphology of C4 leaves is typically modified into Kranz anatomy that consists of repeating units of vein, bundle sheath (BS) and mesophyll (M) cells.
source: The morphology of C4 leaves is typically modified into so-called Kranz anatomy that consists of repeating units of vein, bundle sheath (BS) and mesophyll (M) cells (Hattersley, 1984; Langdale, 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hattersley, 1984 and Langdale, 2011, and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In C4 plants, photosynthetic metabolism becomes modified and compartmentalised between the M and BS, with M cells lacking RuBisCO but containing high activities of PEPC.
source: Photosynthetic metabolism becomes modified and compartmentalised between the M and BS, with M cells lacking RuBisCO but instead containing high activities of the alternate carboxylase PEPC to generate C4 acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis supported by the general literature.

claim: C4 acids are decarboxylated by at least one of three enzymes within BS cells: NADP-ME, NAD-ME, or PCK.
source: C4 acids are decarboxylated by at least one of three enzymes within BS cells: NADP- or NAD-dependent malic enzymes (NADP-ME or NAD-ME respectively), or phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK) (Hatch et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hatch et al., 1975.

claim: Specific lineages of C4 species have typically been classified into one of three sub-types based on the activity of decarboxylases and anatomical and cellular traits.
source: Specific lineages of C4 species have typically been classified into one of three sub-types, based on the activity of these decarboxylases, as well as anatomical and cellular traits that consistently correlate with each other (Furbank, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Furbank, 2011.

claim: The genetic mechanisms underlying the evolution of cell-specific gene expression in C4 plants involve both alterations to cis-elements and trans-acting factors.
source: The genetic mechanisms underlying the evolution of cell-specific gene expression associated with the separation of photosynthetic metabolism between M and BS cells involve both alterations to cis-elements and trans-acting factors (Akyildiz et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2011; Kajala et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Phylogenetically independent lineages of C4 plants have co-opted homologous mechanisms to generate cell specificity.
source: Phylogenetically independent lineages of C4 plants have co-opted homologous mechanisms to generate cell specificity (Brown et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: C3–C4 intermediates are species exhibiting characteristics of both C3 or C4 photosynthesis.
source: Clues to this question exist in the form of C3–C4 intermediates, species exhibiting characteristics of both C3 or C4 photosynthesis, such as the activity or localisation of C4 cycle enzymes (Hattersley and Stone, 1986), the possession of one or more anatomical or cellular adaptations associated with C4 photosynthesis (Moore et al., 1987), or combinations of both (e.g., Kennedy et al., 1980; Kotayeva et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies describing C3-C4 intermediates.

claim: Data was consolidated from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species from 22 genera.
source: To parameterise the phenotypic landscape underlying photosynthetic phenotypes, data was consolidated from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species from 22 genera (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology used in the study.

claim: The C3–C4 species are from 18 independent lineages likely representing 18 distinct evolutionary origins of C3–C4 intermediacy.
source: These C3–C4 species are from 18 independent lineages likely representing 18 distinct evolutionary origins of C3–C4 intermediacy (Sage et al., 2011a) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2011a and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Principal components analysis confirmed the phenotypic intermediacy of the C3–C4 species.
source: Principal components analysis (PCA) was performed to confirm the phenotypic intermediacy of the C3–C4 species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sister-group relationships of C3–C4 species with congeneric C4 clades support the notion that C3–C4 species represent phenotypic states through which transitions to C4 photosynthesis could occur.
source: This result, the sister-group relationships of C3–C4 species with congeneric C4 clades (McKown et al., 2005; Vogan et al., 2007; Christin et al., 2011a; Sage et al., 2011a; Khoshravesh et al., 2012) and the prevalence of extant C3–C4 species in genera with the most recent origins of C4 photosynthesis (Christin et al., 2011b) all support the notion that C3–C4 species represent phenotypic states through which transitions to C4 photosynthesis could occur.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple phylogenetic studies.

claim: The combined traits of C3–C4 intermediate species represent samples from across the space of phenotypes connecting C3 to C4 photosynthesis.
source: The combined traits of C3–C4 intermediate species therefore represent samples from across the space of phenotypes connecting C3 to C4 photosynthesis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the phylogenetic relationships and phenotypic data, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Within the meta-analysis data, C3–C4 phenotypes were available for 33 eudicot and 4 monocot species.
source: Within our meta-analysis data, C3–C4 phenotypes were available for 33 eudicot and 4 monocot species.
evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the dataset.

claim: 16 and 17 of the C3-C4 species have extant congeneric relatives performing NADP-ME or NAD-ME sub-type C4 photosynthesis respectively.
source: 16 and 17 of these species have extant congeneric relatives performing NADP-ME or NAD-ME sub-type C4 photosynthesis respectively.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic relationships of the C3-C4 species in the dataset.

claim: No C3–C4 relatives of PCK sub-type C4 species are known.
source: No C3–C4 relatives of PCK sub-type C4 species are known (Sage et al., 2011a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2011a.

claim: The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and hierarchical clustering were used to impartially assign binary scores to quantitative traits.
source: For quantitative traits the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and hierarchical clustering were used to impartially assign binary scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for data processing, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 16-dimensional phenotype space with 65,536 nodes was defined corresponding to all possible combinations of presence and absence scores for each characteristic.
source: This defined a 16-dimensional phenotype space with 216 (65,536) nodes corresponding to all possible combinations of presence (1) and absence (0) scores for each characteristic.
evidence: This describes the mathematical structure of the phenotype space used in the model.

claim: The phenotypic landscape underlying the evolution of C4 photosynthesis was modelled as a transition network with weighted edges describing the probability of transitions between phenotypic states.
source: The phenotypic landscape underlying the evolution of C4 photosynthesis was then modelled as a transition network, with weighted edges describing the probability of transitions occurring between two phenotypic states (two nodes on the hypercube, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inferential machinery based on Hidden Markov Models was developed to constrain the structure of phenotypic landscapes using observed intermediate points.
source: To do this, we developed inferential machinery based on the framework of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Rabiner, 1989) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This describes the novel methodology developed in the study, with citation to the HMM framework.

claim: A Bayesian MCMC procedure was used to sample from the set of networks most compatible with the meta-analysis dataset.
source: A Bayesian MCMC procedure was used to sample from the set of networks most compatible with the meta-analysis dataset, and thus most likely to represent the underlying dynamics of C4 evolution.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used in the study.

claim: The model imposed that only one C4 trait may be acquired at a time, and loss of acquired C4 traits was forbidden.
source: To model the evolutionary paths generating C4 without requiring additional dimensionality, we imposed that only one C4 trait may be acquired at a time, and loss of acquired C4 traits was forbidden.
evidence: This describes a constraint of the modeling approach.

claim: The approach clearly assigned equal acquisition probabilities to traits whose timing was linked in the underlying dataset, even when 50% of the data was occluded.
source: Our approach clearly assigned equal acquisition probabilities to traits whose timing was linked in the underlying dataset, even when 50% of the data was occluded (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the positive control test shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The approach is able to detect the simultaneous acquisition of traits in evolution, even though single-trait acquisitions are simulated.
source: These data are consistent with this approach detecting the simultaneous acquisition of traits in evolution, even though single-trait acquisitions are simulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the positive control tests.

claim: For 29 occluded traits, 18 were strongly predicted to be present or absent, and of these 18 strongly predicted traits, 15 were correct.
source: For 29 occluded traits 18 were strongly predicted to be present or absent, and the remaining 11 predictions were neutral. Of the 18 strongly predicted traits (i.e., <25% or >75% probability), 15 were correct, with only one false positive and two false negative predictions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the validation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The approach assigns neutral predictions much more frequently than false positive or false negative predictions.
source: The approach therefore assigns neutral predictions much more frequently than false positive or false negative predictions, suggesting that its outputs are highly conservative, and thus unlikely to produce artefacts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results.

claim: Quantitative real-time PCR experimentally verified a subset of predictions relating to abundance of C4 enzymes not previously measured.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR experimentally verified a subset of these, relating to abundance of C4 enzymes not previously measured (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This describes experimental validation shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The results are consistent with previous work proposing that BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism.
source: These results were consistent with previous work on subsets of C4 lineages that proposed the BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism (Hylton et al., 1988; Rawsthorne et al., 1988; Devi et al., 1995; Sage et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of RuBisCO from M cells occurs late in C4 evolution.
source: These results were consistent with previous work on subsets of C4 lineages that proposed the BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism (Hylton et al., 1988; Rawsthorne et al., 1988; Devi et al., 1995; Sage et al., 2012), and loss of RuBisCO from M cells occurs late (Cheng et al., 1988; Khoshravesh et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the model results.

claim: Alterations to leaf anatomy and cell-specificity and increased abundance of multiple C4 cycle enzymes were predicted to evolve prior to any alteration to RuBisCO and PEPC.
source: Alterations to leaf anatomy as well as cell-specificity and increased abundance of multiple C4 cycle enzymes were predicted to evolve prior to any alteration to the primary C3 and C4 photosynthetic enzymes RuBisCO and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was strong evidence for enlargement of BS cells as an early innovation in most C4 lineages.
source: There was also strong evidence for enlargement of BS cells as an early innovation in most C4 lineages (Figure 3), consistent with the suggestion that this was an ancestral state within C3 ancestors of C4 grass lineages and that this contributed to the high number of C4 origins within this family (Christin et al., 2013; Griffiths et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding from Figure 3 is consistent with cited studies on grass lineages.

claim: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times.
source: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times, but for all other C4 enzymes the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claim: For all C4 enzymes except PEPC, the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits.
source: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times, but for all other C4 enzymes the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claim: The result that cell-specificity and increased expression are separated is consistent with molecular analysis showing these are mediated by different cis-elements.
source: This result is consistent with molecular analysis of genes encoding C4 enzymes that indicates cell-specificity and increased expression are mediated by different cis-elements (Akyildiz et al., 2007; Kajala et al., 2012; Wiludda et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: Repeating the analysis using scores assigned by hierarchical clustering did not affect the predicted evolutionary trajectories.
source: First, the analysis was repeated using scores for presence or absence of traits that were assigned by hierarchical clustering, as opposed to using the EM algorithm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). Although hierarchical clustering generated differences in the scoring of a small number of traits, the predicted evolutionary trajectories were not affected, producing highly similar results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removing two independent pairs of traits from the analysis did not affect the predicted timing of the remaining 14 traits.
source: Removing two independent pairs of traits from the analysis did not affect the predicted timing of the remaining 14 traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Including two additional traits associated with C4 photosynthesis did not alter the predicted timing of other traits.
source: Furthermore, including two additional traits associated with C4 photosynthesis also did not alter the predicted timing of other traits (C).
evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The centripetal positioning of mitochondria and the centrifugal or centripetal position of chloroplasts within BS cells are predicted to be acquired early in the evolution of C4 photosynthesis.
source: Consistent with observations made from several genera, we predict that these cellular alterations are acquired early in the evolution of C4 photosynthesis (Hylton et al., 1988; McKown and Dengler, 2007; Muhaidat et al., 2011; Sage et al., 2011b).
evidence: This prediction is consistent with cited observations from multiple genera.

claim: Inflexible linkage between multiple traits was detected in artificial positive control datasets but not in the C3–C4 dataset.
source: Inflexible linkage between multiple traits was detected in artificial positive control datasets (Figure 2B) but not in the C3–C4 dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by comparing results from positive controls (Figure 2B) with the biological data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: The order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible.
source: This result suggests that the order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the contingency analysis showing no inflexible linkage between traits.

claim: Multiple origins of C4 may have been facilitated by flexibility in the evolutionary pathways connecting C3 and C4 phenotypes.
source: Multiple origins of C4 may therefore have been facilitated by this flexibility in the evolutionary pathways connecting C3 and C4 phenotypes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of flexible trait acquisition order.

claim: No single sequence of acquisitions was capable of producing intermediate phenotypes compatible with all observations.
source: First, no single sequence of acquisitions was capable of producing intermediate phenotypes compatible with all observations ('Methods').
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the dynamic programming analysis described in Methods.

claim: Several traits such as compartmentation of GDC into BS and the increased number of chloroplasts in the BS displayed bimodal probability distributions for their acquisition.
source: Second, several traits such as compartmentation of GDC into BS and the increased number of chloroplasts in the BS clearly displayed bimodal probability distributions for their acquisition (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in the probability distributions in Figure 3.

claim: Bimodality in acquisition probabilities is indicative of multiple distinct pathways to C4 photosynthesis that acquire traits at earlier or later times.
source: This bimodality is indicative of multiple distinct pathways to C4 photosynthesis that acquire traits at earlier or later times.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bimodal distributions observed in the data.

claim: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation.
source: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 4A.

claim: The topology of the evolutionary landscape surrounding C4 is largely different for monocots and eudicots.
source: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation (Figure 4A), suggesting that the topology of the evolutionary landscape surrounding C4 is largely different for these two anciently diverged taxa.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The separation between monocot and eudicot evolutionary landscapes is the result of differences in the timing of events generating both anatomical and biochemical traits.
source: Analysis of the posterior probabilities of the mean pathways representing either monocots or dicots revealed that this separation is the result of differences in the timing of events generating both anatomical and biochemical traits (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The ancient divergence of the monocot and eudicot clades constrained the evolution of C4 photosynthesis to broadly different evolutionary pathways in each.
source: We propose that the ancient divergence of the monocot and eudicot clades constrained the evolution of C4 photosynthesis to broadly different evolutionary pathways in each.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed differences between monocot and eudicot pathways.

claim: There was more overlap between the landscapes generating NAD–ME and NADP-ME species than between monocots and eudicots.
source: There was more overlap between the landscapes generating NAD–ME and NADP-ME species (Figure 4B), likely reflecting the convergent origins of NAD–ME and NADP-ME sub-types (Furbank, 2011; Sage et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 4B and interpreted with reference to cited literature.

claim: In NAD–ME lineages, increased vein density was predicted to be acquired early in C4 evolution, while in NADP-ME species this trait showed a broadly different trajectory.
source: For example, in NAD–ME lineages, increased vein density was predicted to be acquired early in C4 evolution, while in NADP-ME species this trait showed a broadly different trajectory (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4D.

claim: The proliferation of chloroplasts in the BS was acquired with different timings between the NAD-ME and NADP-ME sub-types.
source: The proliferation of chloroplasts in the BS was also acquired with different timings between the two sub-types.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of NAD-ME and NADP-ME lineages.

claim: The alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD–ME subtypes were defined by differences in the timing of anatomical and cellular traits that precede the majority of biochemical alterations.
source: The alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD–ME subtypes were therefore defined by differences in the timing of anatomical and cellular traits that are predicted to precede the majority of biochemical alterations (Figure 3, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4D.

claim: Distinct C4 sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in response to non-photosynthetic pressures.
source: We therefore conclude that these distinct sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in response to non-photosynthetic pressures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that anatomical differences precede biochemical differences between subtypes.

claim: Early evolutionary events determined the downstream phenotypes of C4 sub-types by restricting lineages to independent pathways across phenotype space.
source: Furthermore, we propose that early evolutionary events determined the downstream phenotypes of C4 sub-types by restricting lineages to independent pathways across phenotype space.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the evolution of different C4 subtypes.

claim: The novel Bayesian approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference.
source: However, as our approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference, we propose that it could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits, such as those in the fossil record, which are also currently limited by the fragmented nature of data available (Kidwell and Holland, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the developed method.

claim: The approach could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits in the fossil record.
source: However, as our approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference, we propose that it could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits, such as those in the fossil record, which are also currently limited by the fragmented nature of data available (Kidwell and Holland, 2002).
evidence: This is a proposed application of the method with citation to relevant literature.

claim: The approach may be useful in inferring pathways underlying stochastic processes occurring over shorter timescales, such as disease or tumour progression, or cell type differentiation.
source: Our approach is also not limited by the time-scale over which predicted trajectories occur. As a result, it may be useful in inferring pathways underlying stochastic processes occurring over much shorter timescales, such as disease or tumour progression, or the differentiation of cell types.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the method.

claim: According to the hypothesis that declining CO2 drove C4 evolution, alterations to PEPC and RuBisCO would be expected to occur early in the evolutionary trajectories generating C4.
source: A central hypothesis for the ecological drivers of C4 evolution is that declining CO2 concentration in the Oligocene decreased the rate of carboxylation by RuBisCO, creating a strong pressure to evolve alternative photosynthetic strategies (Christin et al., 2008; Vicentini et al., 2008). According to this hypothesis, alterations to the localisation and abundance of the primary carboxylases PEPC and RuBisCO would be expected to occur early in the evolutionary trajectories generating C4.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the cited hypothesis about CO2-driven evolution.

claim: The data suggest that alterations to anatomy and cell biology preceded the majority of biochemical alterations, contrary to the CO2-driven hypothesis.
source: Conversely, our data suggest that alterations to anatomy and cell biology were predicted to precede the majority of biochemical alterations, and that other enzymes of the C4 pathway are recruited prior to PEPC and RuBisCO (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3 that contradicts the CO2-driven hypothesis.

claim: Enzymes such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants.
source: These enzymes, such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases, function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aubry et al., 2011.

claim: The early changes to abundance and localisation of PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases within C4 lineages may have been driven by non-photosynthetic pressures.
source: These enzymes, such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases, function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011), so the early changes to abundance and localisation of these enzymes within C4 lineages may have been driven by non-photosynthetic pressures.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the finding that these enzymes are recruited early and have non-photosynthetic functions.

claim: A recent in silico study predicts that changes to photorespiratory metabolism and GDC in BS cells evolved prior to the C4 pathway.
source: A recent in silico study also predicts that changes to photorespiratory metabolism and GDC in BS cells evolved prior to the C4 pathway (Heckman et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Heckman et al., 2013.

claim: The model predicts that BS-specificity of GDC was acquired early in C4 evolution for the majority of lineages.
source: Our model predicts that BS-specificity of GDC was acquired early in C4 evolution for the majority of lineages.
evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claim: The predicted timing of GDC BS-specificity is bimodal and not predicted to be acquired early in monocot lineages.
source: However, we also note that the predicted timing of GDC BS-specificity is bimodal in our analysis (Figure 3), and not predicted to be acquired early in monocot lineages (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figures 3 and 4C.

claim: BS-specificity of GDC is not a feature of C4 evolution to have occurred repeatedly in all lineages.
source: These results suggest that this is not a feature of C4 evolution to have occurred repeatedly in all lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bimodal distribution and differences between monocots and eudicots.

claim: Recent evidence has identified additional environmental pressures that may have driven C4 evolution, including high evaporative demands and increased fire frequency.
source: Recent evidence from physiological and ecological studies has identified a number of additional environmental pressures that may have driven the evolution and radiation of C4 lineages, including high evaporative demands (Osborne and Sack, 2012) and increased fire frequency (Edwards et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Increased BS volume and vein density have been proposed as likely adaptations to improve leaf hydraulics under drought.
source: Increased BS volume and vein density have been proposed as likely adaptations to improve leaf hydraulics under drought (Osborne and Sack, 2012; Griffiths et al. 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Differences in the timing of events altering leaf vascular development and BS chloroplast division occur prior to the appearance of the alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD-ME biochemical sub-types.
source: For example, we find that differences in the timing of events altering leaf vascular development and BS chloroplast division occur prior to the appearance of the alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD-ME biochemical sub-types (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4D.

claim: These anatomical and cellular traits are predicted to evolve prior to any alterations to the C4 acid decarboxylase enzymes that traditionally define the NADP-ME and NAD-ME sub-types.
source: These traits are predicted to evolve prior to any alterations to the C4 acid decarboxylase enzymes that traditionally define these sub-types (Furbank, 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the model with reference to the traditional classification.

claim: An homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages.
source: As an homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages (Brown et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: It is unlikely that mechanisms underlying the recruitment of decarboxylase enzymes drove the evolution of distinct C4 sub-types.
source: As an homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages (Brown et al., 2011), it is unlikely that mechanisms underlying the recruitment of these enzymes drove the evolution of distinct sub-types.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of homologous mechanisms and the timing of trait acquisition.

claim: Different C4 sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in leaf development, rather than biochemical or photosynthetic pressures.
source: We therefore conclude that these different sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in leaf development, rather than biochemical or photosynthetic pressures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that anatomical differences precede biochemical differences.

claim: Differences in the carboxylation efficiency or photosynthetic performance of different C4 sub-types have never been detected.
source: This may explain why differences in the carboxylation efficiency or photosynthetic performance of different C4 sub-types have never been detected (Furbank, 2011), making the adaptive significance of different decarboxylation mechanisms difficult to explain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Furbank, 2011.

claim: At least four distinct evolutionary trajectories underlie the evolution of C4 lineages.
source: First, we show that at least four distinct evolutionary trajectories underlie the evolution of C4 lineages (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the comparative analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: There is no evidence for inflexible linkage between the predicted timing of distinct C4 traits.
source: Second, we find no evidence for inflexible linkage between the predicted timing of distinct C4 traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the contingency analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 (note: the text says supplement 1 but likely refers to supplement 3).

claim: Diversity in viable pathways helps explain why C4 has been accessible to such a wide variety of species.
source: This diversity in viable pathways also helps explain why C4 has been accessible to such a wide variety of species and not limited to a smaller subset of the angiosperm phylogeny.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of multiple flexible pathways.
